prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, through Katori's magic-wavelength trapping concept and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock (B019) with Katori and Ye, and the second round has strengthened rather than weakened my reasons. The chair asks what is discovered beyond better numbers. My answer is this: the magic-wavelength condition is a physical statement that a trapping potential can be chosen so that it does not perturb the clock transition to first order, which lets very many atoms be held without Doppler or recoil shifts and interrogated in parallel. That is a new regime of observation, because once systematic uncertainty went below about 10^-17 the instrument became a probe of nature: it resolves the gravitational redshift across a millimetre, bounds drifts of fundamental constants, and makes many-body shifts a measurable quantity. This is the kind of clue from nature I look for in a prize, and the discovery is reproduced and compared at RIKEN, JILA, SYRTE, PTB and NIST with agreed uncertainty budgets, so its interpretation is closed. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: the concept and first demonstration are Katori's, the many-body and systematics frontier is Ye's. I would word the citation around the instrument and its physics and leave the redefinition of the second out of both citation and rationale; that decision belongs to metrology bodies and is prospective.
statement.case_against: The serious objection is overlap and incrementalism. The 2005 frequency comb, the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems, and laser cooling in 1997 and 2018 already honoured the toolbox, and a committee could fairly read lattice clocks as the long refinement of a prized line. Mehlig ranked it only sixth on this ground, and several of its own supporters list the same overlap among their reservations. Credit is also not airtight: the first Sr lattice-clock priority (Tokyo, JILA, SYRTE) has not been checked against the record, and Lemonde, Derevianko and the ion-clock groups are outside the pair. Finally, two members (Johansson and I) moved here after reading the other ballots, so part of the support is recent, and my declared dark-energy bias should not make me undervalue B016 or overvalue a result that merely seems tidy.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked the lattice clocks sixth and, in his reply to Kroll, calls the clock an instrument achievement built on the frequency comb, whereas magic-angle graphene is a new regime of matter.
responses.response: I take this distinction seriously and it is the main open question for B019, but I think it is answered by what the instrument did once it worked. The comb counts optical cycles; the magic-wavelength lattice makes the atoms themselves an almost unperturbed reference and allows N-atom statistics with a vanishing systematic. The step from 10^-16 to 10^-18 needed that, plus control of collisions and many-body shifts, and none of it is in the 2005 or 2012 citations. I would still not claim that a precision threshold is by itself a discovery. What persuades me is that the machine now measures something new, such as the redshift over a millimetre and the constancy of constants. I agree with you that B047 describes a new regime of matter, and that is why it remains my first alternative, but I would not rank it above B019 this year.

responses.point: Olsson argues that waiting on B047 is not neutral because the evidence is in, and that the pairing mechanism is a follow-up question, not part of what was discovered; she names Bistritzer with MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero.
responses.response: I find that argument stronger than I did in round 1, and I now accept that a prize for B047 would not need a settled pairing mechanism if the citation were limited to the flat-band prediction and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting phases. Two things still hold me back. First, twist-angle disorder and sample-to-sample variation limit the quantitative comparison of theory and experiment, so the stability of interpretation is lower than for a clock budget confirmed by several institutes. Second, I share your own unease about the experimental credit: naming Jarillo-Herrero alone while Cao, Fatemi and others made the 2018 measurements is hard to defend with certainty, and I would want the committee to check the 2018 author contributions and parallel moire priorities first. If outside experts report that the author record supports a single experimental name, I would move B047 up; for now it stays as an alternative, not a preferred part.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B012 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp), valuing more than fifteen years of independent confirmation and a stable interpretation, and distinguishes the Z2 state from the 2016 topological prize.
responses.response: I accept that the Z2 quantum spin Hall state is distinct from the integer quantum Hall topology of 2016, and that maturity is the strongest part of your case; that argument deserves weight and I have not dismissed it. What keeps me from moving is the credit. You and I both agree that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route Molenkamp realised, that Zhang has died, and that the 3D pioneers cannot be added within three names. A narrow citation to the two-dimensional effect avoids the 3D problem, but it leaves a prize in which the experimentalist verified a prediction whose author is outside the set. For B019 the corresponding gaps (Lemonde, Derevianko) are about the periphery, not the central proposal. I would rank B012 behind both B019 and B047 and I would not object to it in a later cycle.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asks what is new beyond better numbers for B019 and whether the committee should verify lattice-clock priority and the status of Lemonde and Derevianko before the final ballot.
responses.response: On the first question, my one-sentence answer is that the magic-wavelength lattice turned atomic clocks from single-particle references into many-atom quantum systems with a cancelled trap shift, and the resulting 10^-18 level is what lets the instrument test relativity and constants. On the second, I would support a short check of the priority record for the first Sr lattice clock at Tokyo, JILA and SYRTE, and of the role of Lemonde and Derevianko, but I would treat it as confirmation of the pair, not as a reason to widen it. Theory identifying magic wavelengths and shifts is real work, but the prize should go to the proposal and the demonstration. I also agree with you and with Kroll that the redefinition of the second belongs outside the case.

responses.point: Kroll wants the B019 citation to name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly so the comb overlap is not an issue, and asks for the priority record of early Sr lattice-clock measurements to be checked.
responses.response: I agree on both points. The citation I now propose names the magic-wavelength concept and its realisation at the 10^-18 level, which lets the text itself show the difference from the 2005 prize. On priority, I would ask the committee to commission the check you describe before the final ballot, since a dispute there is the most likely place for a credit problem. Where I would stay cautious is your remark that only a few members ranked it first at the opening: breadth of support is not a scientific argument, and I would not use it to defend the clock.

uncertainties: Whether outside evaluation of the first Sr lattice-clock priority (Katori, JILA, SYRTE) and of Lemonde and Derevianko leaves Katori and Ye intact as the pair.
Whether the committee accepts that crossing 10^-17 to 10^-18 with a magic-wavelength lattice is a discovery of new physics capability and not a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
Whether B047 can be prized on the flat-band prediction and the correlated phases alone, and whether a check of the 2018 author record would change the experimental credit.
How BAO (B016) should be viewed if the DESI hints of evolving dark energy firm up; I keep it as an alternative but judge it less cleanly attributable this year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted name, including Katori and Ye. My PhD supervisor (Gross), my mentor (Rubinstein) and my co-author (Van Riet) are not connected to any candidate. I continue to declare that my research interest in dark energy may bias me toward B016, which I have placed as an alternative and not as my preferred part; I note this so that colleagues can discount it.
